observations.subject: economics
failure_details: D is the textbook definition: an economy-wide rise in the propensity to save does not raise aggregate saving; it may leave it unchanged or reduce it (E1.1).

However, in the standard two-sector model with autonomous expenditure/investment held fixed, equilibrium saving equals autonomous investment: from Y = C₀ + cY + I, S = Y − C₀ − cY = I. Changing c can therefore leave aggregate saving unchanged. This makes A, B and C potentially true as outcome statements in that model, even though D alone states the named paradox’s defining trigger.

The source gives the paradox within the income-determination model (E1.5, E2.1), but the item does not identify that model or qualify its alternatives. This weakens the one-answer quality under a strict reading.

Defect: Options A, B and C are not unambiguously false as propositions in the standard two-sector model with autonomous expenditure/investment held fixed: equilibrium aggregate saving remains equal to fixed investment when the saving/consumption propensity changes. The model qualification is unstated, creating competing plausible claims despite D being the textbook definition.
Defect: The stem states the paradox as a general definition, while the supplied textbook treatment derives the result within its income-determination model; the model scope is not made explicit.
